newsitem.title: ALBANIA: ALBANIA LEADERS DROP EMERGENCY RULE IN RIOT CITY.
newsitem.headline: ALBANIA LEADERS DROP EMERGENCY RULE IN RIOT CITY.

text.p: Albania's leadership appeared to back away from a plan to proclaim emergency rule in the southern port of Vlore, where three people died in rioting this week, after deputies from the region denounced the move.

Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi, in a telephone interview late on Tuesday, said his administration was trying to restore peace through dialogue in the city, quiet after two days of battles between police and anti-government protesters.
"Considering the situation in Vlore, the deputies from Vlore thought it was better not to adopt this law," Meksi said in English.
"This was our proposal, but we decided this evening to postpone the law. We hope to change the attitude and develop a dialogue between the government and the Vlore people."

Meksi had proposed emergency measures, including deployment of the army, after blaming leftist extremists for the unrest sparked by the collapse of pyramid investment schemes with the life savings of hundreds of thousands of people.
In Vlore, at least 30,000 mourners streamed through the streets in an outpouring of emotion at the funeral of a 33-year-old shop owner killed in the fiercest clashes on Monday.
Marchers shouted "The police killed him!" and blamed President Sali Berisha for the loss of what little money they had accumulated in Europe's poorest country.
As the cortege accompanied the open coffin down to the harbour, mourners cheered as the local headquarters of Berisha's Democratic Party was consumed by flames.
There was no indication what caused the blaze. The party is reviled by the protesters, some of whom say it used money from the funds to finance its re-election campaign last year.

Some 10,000 demonstrators later massed in a square in what is now an evening ritual, but they dispersed without incident. Police appeared to abandon the city altogether, including their main station, site of some of this week's most bitter fighting.
Albania's neighbours offered to seek international support.

Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini said Rome was sounding out other countries on the prospects of aid. A spokesman for Greece's foreign ministry said Athens would ask the European Union to help Albania and Bulgaria.

In parliament, deputies had considered for two days a law on emergency measures and then how to apply it to the situation in Vlore. In the end, it was the Democratic Party's own members from Vlore who refused to accept emergency rule in the city.

"As deputies for Vlore, we cannot send troops and tanks into our city," Dashamir Shehi, a former deputy prime minister, said after the debate. "Laws have been broken but there is always room for dialogue. This is not solved with truncheons."
Meksi, who has played an increasingly prominent role in recent weeks, said the party leadership would discuss further strategy on Wednesday. He renewed proposals to meet opposition parties.
"Some people are thinking in a different way but I think we are united," he said.

The Forum for Democracy opposition alliance stayed away from talks with authorities last week to discuss the pyramid scandal on grounds that it was a "publicity stunt". But it favours dialogue in order to form a "technocrat government".
The Forum scheduled a rally for Wednesday in a Tirana stadium. But authorities banned it and its leaders were uncertain about whether to proceed.

About 150 demonstrators briefly shouted "Vlore! Vlore!" in Tirana's central Skanderbeg Square on Tuesday, then scattered to dodge truckloads of riot police. Police with batons broke up an opposition rally in Tirana last weekend.
